The history of computing is long and varied. Early mechanical devices like the abacus date back thousands of years. In the 19th century, Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and later the Analytical Engine, the latter being a general-purpose mechanical computer. Ada Lovelace wrote what is considered the first algorithm intended to be processed by a machine.

In the 20th century, Alan Turing formalised the concept of computation with the Turing machine. During World War II, Colossus was built at Bletchley Park to crack German ciphers. ENIAC, completed in 1945, is often cited as the first general-purpose electronic digital computer, though this is disputed.

The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947 by Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley, replaced vacuum tubes and made smaller, faster, more reliable computers possible. Integrated circuits followed in the late 1950s, pioneered by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor.

The microprocessor arrived in 1971 with Intel's 4004, designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stan Mazor. This led to the personal computer revolution of the 1980s. The Altair 8800 (1975) inspired Bill Gates and Paul Allen to found Microsoft. The Apple II (1977) and IBM PC (1981) brought computing to homes and offices.

The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN, initially as a way to share documents between researchers. The first web browser, WorldWideWeb (later renamed Nexus), was also written by Berners-Lee.

In the 2000s, mobile computing exploded. The iPhone launched in 2007, fundamentally changing how people interact with computers. Cloud computing, where resources are delivered over the internet, became dominant in enterprise by the 2010s.

Artificial intelligence research, which had been ongoing since the 1950s, saw a resurgence in the 2010s driven by deep learning, large datasets, and GPU acceleration. The transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', became the foundation for modern large language models.
